info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 14.2: Automated Alignment with CollateX.

questiontext.text: How does the intellectual labour of automated collation differ fundamentally from manual collation on paper?

generalfeedback.text: Configuration is not a smaller task than manual collation, but a different one — stating as a rule what you decided case by case.

answer.text: Manual collation applies tacit judgement case by case during reading, whereas automated collation requires formalizing those judgements in advance as explicit rules and configuration.

feedback.text: Correct. The philological burden does not disappear; it shifts from real-time sequential evaluation to upfront data modeling, tokenization rules, and normalization design.

answer.text: Automated collation eliminates the need for any philological knowledge because the software interprets meaning autonomously.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Computers are strictly literal; without explicit human configuration, algorithms flag trivial orthographic noise as substantive variants.

answer.text: Automated collation requires fewer editorial decisions because software defaults are universally accurate for all manuscript traditions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Default settings almost always produce noise; every decision must be explicitly parameterized by the editor.

answer.text: Manual collation is mathematically reproducible, whereas automated collation varies with each run.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Deterministic software produces exact mathematical reproducibility, which manual reading cannot achieve.

questiontext.text: Why does the Gothenburg Model strictly separate the Normalization stage from the Alignment stage in automated collation?

generalfeedback.text: Alignment is the solved part; tokenization and normalization are where the philology goes, and they are where you will spend today.

answer.text: It allows non-significant variation to be neutralized in a secondary processing layer for matching without altering the underlying archival transcription.

feedback.text: Correct. The five-stage pipeline ensures the diplomatic text is preserved untouched while a derived, normalized representation is passed to the alignment algorithm.

answer.text: Separating normalization forces the alignment engine to discard all witness sigla.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Witness sigla are preserved across all stages to track reading attributions.

answer.text: It enables the alignment algorithm to modify the original TEI XML files directly on disk.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Normalization creates temporary computational representations; it never overwrites source files.

answer.text: Dynamic programming cannot execute if tokenization occurs in the same script as alignment.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The separation of concerns is architectural and modular, not a language limitation.

questiontext.text: How does the Needleman–Wunsch algorithm relate mathematically to the Wagner–Fischer edit-distance algorithm from Lesson 5.2?

generalfeedback.text: Needleman–Wunsch is the same dynamic programming as Wagner–Fischer, maximizing alignment score rather than minimizing edit distance.

answer.text: Both use dynamic programming matrices over sequence pairs, but Wagner–Fischer minimizes an edit distance while Needleman–Wunsch maximizes a global alignment score.

feedback.text: Correct. They share the same underlying dynamic programming structure and matrix traceback, directed toward complementary optimization goals.

answer.text: Needleman–Wunsch uses neural embeddings, whereas Wagner–Fischer is deterministic.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both are classical, deterministic dynamic programming algorithms.

answer.text: Wagner–Fischer aligns entire documents globally, whereas Needleman–Wunsch only aligns individual letters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Needleman–Wunsch is designed specifically for optimal global sequence alignment.

answer.text: Needleman–Wunsch replaces scoring matrices with random Monte Carlo sampling.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Needleman–Wunsch is an exact, non-probabilistic matrix algorithm.

name.text: 04 Question: Affine Gap Penalties and Scribal Reality

questiontext.text: Why is an affine gap penalty model philologically superior to a linear gap penalty model when collating manuscripts?

generalfeedback.text: Affine gap penalties encode the philological claim that omissions are single events — which is why the algorithm finds them as gaps rather than as scattered mismatches.

answer.text: It charges a heavy penalty for opening a gap and a small penalty for extending it, correctly modeling a multi-word scribal omission as a single cognitive event.

feedback.text: Correct. Scribal omissions (such as homoioteleuton) happen in a single eye-skip; linear penalties treat a ten-word gap as ten independent errors, often forcing spurious matches.

answer.text: It ensures that omissions are completely hidden from the critical apparatus.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Omissions are cleanly detected and highlighted as continuous blocks.

answer.text: It reduces the computational time complexity from O(mn) to O(1).

feedback.text: Incorrect. Affine gap calculations still run in polynomial dynamic programming time.

answer.text: It automatically identifies the exact authorial reading without editorial review.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Gap scoring optimizes sequence alignment, not editorial adjudication.

questiontext.text: What is the structural advantage of using a directed acyclic graph (DAG) to represent multi-witness collations in CollateX?

generalfeedback.text: A variant graph represents all witnesses in one acyclic structure with no base text — which is the structural answer to base-text bias.

answer.text: It represents all witnesses simultaneously in a single unified structure without privileging any witness as an arbitrary base text.

feedback.text: Correct. Witnesses share nodes where they agree and branch where they diverge; acyclicity strictly preserves linear reading order without base-text bias.

answer.text: It allows the text to form recursive feedback loops that generate new poetic verses.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Acyclicity specifically prevents loops in order to preserve linear reading sequence.

answer.text: It automatically translates medieval Greek into modern vernacular English during traversal.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The variant graph models textual topology, not natural language translation.

answer.text: It eliminates the need for Unicode UTF-8 encoding across manuscript nodes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Graph nodes store standard UTF-8 string tokens.

questiontext.text: How does progressive multiple alignment in CollateX incorporate additional witnesses beyond the initial pair?

generalfeedback.text: Progressive alignment merges each witness into an accumulated graph rather than comparing against a base — which removes the bias but makes witness order slightly significant.

answer.text: Each new witness is aligned sequentially against the accumulated variant graph rather than against a single historical base text.

feedback.text: Correct. Progressive alignment merges witnesses into the growing graph, eliminating base-text bias (though witness addition order can exert subtle effects).

answer.text: Every witness is compared against a hardcoded 19th-century printed edition stored on a central server.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CollateX aligns against the emerging consensus graph of the supplied witnesses.

answer.text: CollateX generates every possible combinatorial tree permutation before selecting the median.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Full combinatorial alignment is computationally intractable; progressive alignment aligns iteratively.

answer.text: New witnesses overwrite previous witnesses whenever a disagreement is encountered.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Disagreements create branching paths labeled with respective witness sigla.

name.text: 07 Question: A First, Deliberately Unconfigured Run

questiontext.text: What is the primary diagnostic value of running CollateX on raw, un-normalized witness texts before applying any configuration?

generalfeedback.text: Run unconfigured first and investigate every difference that appears in neither of your lists — those are what your attention missed.

answer.text: It exposes the baseline noise and reveals genuine variants that fatigued human attention missed during manual collation.

feedback.text: Correct. Seeing differences that appear in neither your manual variant list nor your discounted list flags missed variants and exposes how tokenization defaults behave.

answer.text: It validates the TEI XML schema files against the W3C consortium rules.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schema validation is done with XML parsers, not by running unconfigured CollateX.

answer.text: It proves that automated collation requires no further human intervention or adjustment.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The unconfigured run produces a heavily fragmented, noisy graph that demonstrates why configuration is essential.

answer.text: It permanently encrypts the raw transcriptions to prevent unauthorized student copying.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The unconfigured run is an analytical baseline, not an encryption step.

questiontext.text: What happens during automated collation if a tokenizer fails to rejoin words hyphenated across manuscript line breaks?

generalfeedback.text: Rejoin line-broken words in the tokenizer or your witnesses will differ at every line break — a large source of entirely spurious variants.

answer.text: The algorithm treats the broken fragments as distinct tokens, generating spurious variant mismatches at every line ending where witnesses break differently.

feedback.text: Correct. Lineation varies between manuscripts; unless line-broken words are rejoined (e.g. λό-\nγος -> λόγος), line breaks masquerade as substantive textual variants.

answer.text: The Python interpreter crashes with a buffer overflow exception.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The script executes normally, but produces thousands of false variant entries.

answer.text: All vowels in the document are automatically converted to uppercase Greek capitals.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tokenization splits strings; it does not alter letter casing.

answer.text: CollateX automatically deletes the entire paragraph containing the line break.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CollateX aligns the broken tokens as individual mismatches.

name.text: 09 Question: Dual-Token JSON: The t and n Values

questiontext.text: In CollateX's dual-token JSON input format, what is the distinct role of the n property compared to the t property?

generalfeedback.text: The n value is only for matching and never reaches the reader, so reduce it to exactly the features you consider alignment-significant.

answer.text: The n value is used strictly by the algorithm for matching and alignment, while t preserves the archival diplomatic surface form for the reader.

feedback.text: Correct. By reducing n (e.g., lowercasing, stripping accents/punctuation), differing spellings align cleanly while their authentic diplomatic text is retained in t.

answer.text: The n property stores line numbers, while t stores timestamp metadata.

feedback.text: Incorrect. n stands for normalized matching string, and t stands for token text.

answer.text: The t property is passed to machine translation APIs, while n is deleted after import.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both properties are retained; t is rendered in output tables and TEI exports.

answer.text: The n value is published in the critical apparatus, while t is permanently hidden.

feedback.text: Incorrect. t provides the actual readings displayed in the apparatus.

name.text: 10 Question: Encoding Your Discounted List as Normalization

questiontext.text: Why must every reduction applied to the n matching value (such as diacritic stripping or lowercasing) be recorded in the method document?

generalfeedback.text: Each reduction applied to the n value is an editorial claim that a class of difference does not count — record them all.

answer.text: Each reduction represents an explicit editorial claim that a specific category of variation carries zero substantive or stemmatic significance.

feedback.text: Correct. Normalization is not neutral preprocessing; it embodies theoretical claims about which features matter for establishing the text.

answer.text: The Unicode Consortium legally requires all diacritic removal scripts to be registered publicly.

feedback.text: Incorrect. There are no legal registry requirements; recording normalization is an editorial responsibility.

answer.text: Unrecorded normalization scripts cause Git repositories to fail checksum integrity verification.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git tracks file changes regardless of philological documentation.

answer.text: CollateX cannot parse XML entities unless they are listed in a markdown comment.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Method documentation is for human scholars to understand what question the collation answers.

questiontext.text: What is the primary danger of enabling Levenshtein distance fuzzy matching (near_match=True) instead of explicit dual-token normalization?

generalfeedback.text: Fuzzy matching aligns coincidentally similar words — prefer dual-token normalization, since Week 6 already did the expensive part.

answer.text: It risks aligning distinct, substantive words that coincidentally share similar spelling, introducing false positives into the apparatus.

feedback.text: Correct. Edit distance cannot distinguish an orthographic spelling variant from two entirely different short words that differ by one character.

answer.text: It increases memory usage beyond the capacity of modern 64-bit operating systems.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Levenshtein calculations are lightweight; the danger is philological false matching.

answer.text: It forces CollateX to convert all Greek characters into Latin phonetic equivalents.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Fuzzy matching calculates character edit distance within the native script.

answer.text: It deletes all punctuation marks from the source TEI documents permanently.

feedback.text: Incorrect. near_match is an alignment parameter, not a file deletion tool.

questiontext.text: Why should near_match be set to False when running CollateX with carefully prepared dual-token JSON?

generalfeedback.text: Disable near_match when you have normalized deliberately — it keeps alignment governed by your decisions rather than a distance threshold.

answer.text: Because alignment should be strictly governed by the editor's explicit normalization rules rather than by an arbitrary edit-distance threshold.

feedback.text: Correct. When n values already encode your regularized decisions, disabling fuzzy matching prevents spurious accidental alignments.

answer.text: Because setting near_match=False accelerates collation speed by a factor of one million.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Speed is not the primary rationale; governing alignment by deliberate philological policy is.

answer.text: Because CollateX crashes if dual tokens and fuzzy matching are enabled simultaneously.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CollateX supports both, but disabling fuzzy matching ensures deterministic rule-based alignment.

answer.text: Because TEI parallel segmentation cannot encode entries produced without fuzzy matching.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI export functions identically under strict and fuzzy alignment modes.

name.text: 13 Question: Measuring Against the Manual Collation

questiontext.text: When comparing configured CollateX output against your manual baseline, what does a low precision score typically indicate?

generalfeedback.text: Low precision usually means your configuration is incomplete rather than that the tool is over-reporting — check that first.

answer.text: The normalization configuration is incomplete, causing the tool to report differences that you intended to discount.

feedback.text: Correct. Low precision means the tool is reporting many non-substantive differences; checking your discounting rules will identify what normalization missed.

answer.text: The alignment algorithm has suffered permanent bit-rot in its local Python library cache.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Software does not suffer bit-rot; low precision reflects unencoded discounting policies.

answer.text: The manual collation was 100% erroneous and must be discarded immediately.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The manual collation is the reference standard; discrepancies highlight configuration gaps.

answer.text: The manuscript witnesses belong to entirely different literary works.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Low precision in a known passage is a tuning and filtering issue, not a text identity failure.

name.text: 14 Question: How the Algorithm Handled Your Omission

questiontext.text: When evaluating CollateX's handling of a known homoioteleuton omission, what does slight ambiguity in gap boundary placement indicate?

generalfeedback.text: Ambiguous gap boundaries where the boundary word repeats corroborate a homoioteleuton diagnosis rather than indicating an alignment failure.

answer.text: The boundary words repeat in the text, corroborating that the omission was caused by scribal eye-skip between identical forms.

feedback.text: Correct. Where identical words flank an omission, multiple alignment paths yield identical scores, which is physical evidence of homoioteleuton.

answer.text: The dynamic programming matrix encountered a floating-point calculation error.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Sequence alignment uses integer score additions, not floating-point rounding errors.

answer.text: CollateX failed to implement the Needleman–Wunsch algorithm correctly.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Multiple valid traceback paths are an inherent property of sequence alignment across repeated tokens.

answer.text: The scribe erased the parchment with chemical acid prior to binding.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Boundary ambiguity arises from textual repetition, not chemical erasure.

name.text: 15 Question: How the Algorithm Handled Your Transposition

questiontext.text: Why does CollateX report a transposed sentence as a separate deletion in one place and an insertion in another rather than a single event?

generalfeedback.text: The DAG cannot express a backward move, so a transposition arrives as two entries where one editorial fact exists — and correcting that is manual.

answer.text: The underlying variant graph cannot contain backward cycles to represent moved text without breaking the DAG acyclicity constraint.

feedback.text: Correct. Preserving linear traversal prevents cycles; moved text can only be flagged by secondary heuristic metadata, arriving in the core alignment as two separate operations.

answer.text: CollateX was programmed specifically to punish scribes who altered word order.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The limitation is mathematical and structural, not an intentional punishment.

answer.text: Transposed text contains invisible Unicode control characters that break graph nodes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Transpositions are composed of regular word tokens; the constraint is graph topology.

answer.text: The Python CSV export library does not support multi-line text strings.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CSV supports multiline fields; the limitation is inside the variant graph model itself.

questiontext.text: During configuration tuning, what is indicated if an adjustment causes both the total reported differences AND your recorded true variants to drop?

generalfeedback.text: A configuration step that reduces both reported differences and recorded variants is over-normalizing — check that no real variant disappeared.

answer.text: The configuration is over-normalizing, inadvertently collapsing substantive distinctions that carry philological significance.

feedback.text: Correct. If true variants disappear from the output, your normalization rules (e.g. aggressive diacritic or stem stripping) are too destructive.

answer.text: The alignment algorithm has achieved optimal mathematical perfection.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Losing real variants is a failure of recall, not perfection.

answer.text: The computer processor has run out of dynamic memory allocation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Memory exhaustion produces error crashes, not filtered variant outputs.

answer.text: The TEI XML source file has been restored to its factory default state.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The issue is over-aggressive normalization in the collation script.

name.text: 17 Question: Case Study: Scaling to Eleven Million Words

questiontext.text: What did the 7PartidasDigital project demonstrate regarding automated collation at massive scale?

generalfeedback.text: At eleven million words automation is not better than manual collation — it is the only option, and it reveals patterns sequential reading cannot.

answer.text: Automating alignment with CollateX enabled the detection of subtle linguistic retrogressions across 100 witnesses that sequential manual reading could never have uncovered.

feedback.text: Correct. At 11 million words, manual collation is impossible; automated alignment across massive corpora reveals macro-level transmission patterns invisible to human readers.

answer.text: Spreadsheet color-coding is more efficient than Python scripts for traditions exceeding 50 witnesses.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manual spreadsheet methods completely broke down under the scale of the Siete Partidas.

answer.text: Language models can collate medieval Spanish without requiring tokenization or normalization.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The project relied on deterministic CollateX pipelines with explicit normalization.

answer.text: Automated collation completely eliminates the need for manual editorial adjudication of variants.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Automated alignment produced CSV matrices that scholars then adjudicated by hand.

name.text: 18 Question: Case Study: Comparing the Tools

questiontext.text: Why did comparative tool evaluations (such as Mabille's study on the Fuero Juzgo) conclude that CollateX was superior to Juxta and Stemmaweb for rigorous critical editing?

generalfeedback.text: Collation tools differ less in their algorithms than in whether they let the editor express philological distinctions before and after alignment.

answer.text: CollateX allows flexible pre-alignment JSON normalization and exports editable matrices, whereas Juxta suffered from base-text bias and Stemmaweb conflated orthographic and substantive variants.

feedback.text: Correct. The primary differentiator among collation tools is whether they let editors model and separate philological layers before and after alignment.

answer.text: CollateX features a proprietary 3D virtual reality interface for reading medieval manuscripts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CollateX is a scriptable Python library focused on rigorous data processing, not VR.

answer.text: Juxta and Stemmaweb are written in obsolete assembly code that cannot run on modern computers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The tools operate on modern systems; their limitations were architectural and methodological.

answer.text: CollateX automatically writes the complete editorial commentary without human oversight.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CollateX provides alignment data; editorial commentary remains human scholarship.

questiontext.text: What essential editorial components are intentionally ABSENT from CollateX's raw TEI parallel segmentation export?

generalfeedback.text: The TEI export records that witnesses differ but not which reading is adopted or how significant it is — both are Week 8's editorial work.

answer.text: The adopted reading (), the variant classification, and the contextual commentary.

feedback.text: Correct. CollateX exports neutral variation ( with elements); selecting the lemma, filtering by significance, and adding commentary are Week 8's editorial tasks.

answer.text: The witness sigla attributes and XML closing tags.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CollateX generates fully valid XML with @wit sigla attributes.

answer.text: The text of the manuscript readings in Witness A and Witness B.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The readings are present inside elements.

answer.text: The UTF-8 encoding declaration in the XML prolog.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Standard XML headers are included in export outputs.

questiontext.text: Why is complete methodological reproducibility achievable for CollateX alignment in a way that is not possible for manual collation or generative AI?

generalfeedback.text: The configuration is a finite list of explicit decisions, so complete reproducibility is achievable here in a way it will not be on Friday.

answer.text: The collation is executed by a deterministic algorithm governed by a finite list of explicit, committed code rules and parameters.

feedback.text: Correct. Anyone running the same committed script on the same input files will produce the exact same alignment bit for bit.

answer.text: Because CollateX outputs are legally copyrighted under international open-access treaties.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Reproducibility is a technical property of deterministic code, not a legal treaty.

answer.text: Because manual collation records are deleted upon submission to the course instructor.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manual records are preserved, but human attention cannot be deterministically re-executed.

answer.text: Because language models require daily subscription fees to reproduce outputs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Generative models are stochastic; CollateX is deterministic and local.

name.text: 21 Question: What the Algorithm Cannot Do

questiontext.text: Why does a deterministic sequence alignment engine fail to recognize synonym substitutions as semantically related variants?

generalfeedback.text: The algorithm aligns by character overlap and has no semantic comprehension — a synonym substitution registers as divergence without being recognized as one.

answer.text: It operates purely on character overlap and string equality; without semantic comprehension, two words sharing no letters appear as unrelated divergence.

feedback.text: Correct. CollateX has no linguistic model of meaning; a scribe substituting a synonym is aligned strictly by character matching or pre-coded dictionary equivalence.

answer.text: It cannot parse non-Latin character sets in modern operating systems.

feedback.text: Incorrect. UTF-8 characters are parsed cleanly; the limitation is semantic blindness.

answer.text: It deletes any word that has more than one synonym in Greek lexicons.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Words are never deleted; they are aligned as mismatches.

answer.text: Dynamic programming only works on numeric integers rather than alphabetic text strings.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Character sequences are mapped to matrix indices during alignment.

questiontext.text: Before accepting an improved precision score after refining your normalization configuration, what critical verification must be performed?

generalfeedback.text: Verify that no recorded variant disappeared under normalization before accepting an improved precision figure.

answer.text: Verify that no genuine, recorded variant from your manual baseline was inadvertently suppressed by over-aggressive normalization.

feedback.text: Correct. High precision is meaningless if recall drops; you must ensure that eliminating noise did not eliminate real substantive variants.

answer.text: Ensure that the CSV export file size is an exact multiple of 1024 bytes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. File byte boundaries have no bearing on philological precision.

answer.text: Check that both manuscript facsimiles have been deleted from the local disk cache.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Facsimiles must be retained for continuous verification.

answer.text: Confirm that all Greek verbs have been translated into Latin third-person plurals.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Greek texts remain in their original language and grammatical forms.

questiontext.text: If a configured CollateX run reports almost zero variants across a heavily contested passage, what is the most likely error?

generalfeedback.text: Few reported variants looks like a clean result and may mean your normalization collapsed real distinctions — verify against the manual record.

answer.text: Over-aggressive normalization that stripped significant stems, prefixes, or grammatical endings, collapsing real differences into false matches.

feedback.text: Correct. An output with suspiciously few variants usually means the n reduction rules were too broad, destroying meaningful distinctions.

answer.text: The alignment algorithm ran out of CPU cycles and skipped the middle of the text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Algorithms do not skip text due to cycle limits; over-normalization is the culprit.

answer.text: The manuscript witnesses were automatically merged by Git into a single file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CollateX operates on distinct witness inputs; Git does not merge input data unprompted.

answer.text: The Greek text was written in an uncial hand that cannot be aligned computationally.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Letter hand style does not affect digital string alignment once transcribed.

name.text: 24 Question: What Good Work Looks Like Here

questiontext.text: What turns a mechanical measurement of CollateX performance into a genuine scholarly contribution to your edition?

generalfeedback.text: Reporting the variants the tool found that you missed is what turns a measurement of the tool into an improvement of the edition.

answer.text: Identifying variants the tool found that human fatigue missed during manual collation, and verifying them against manuscript facsimiles to improve the edition.

feedback.text: Correct. Using uniform machine attention to catch human oversight demonstrates how computational methods actively refine editorial scholarship.

answer.text: Manually editing the CSV output to force 100% agreement with pre-conceived theories.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Forcing data to match theories corrupts the evidential record.

answer.text: Deleting the manual collation record so that only computational results survive.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The manual baseline is essential for proving how the automated result was validated.

answer.text: Generating 3D animated bar charts of word lengths for the course presentation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. High-quality work focuses on philological verification, not decorative graphics.

questiontext.text: Why does testing generative language models on transpositions provide a sharp evaluation of semantic reasoning versus variant graphs?

generalfeedback.text: Whether a model recognizes your transposition as one event tests directly whether semantic reasoning supplies what the graph model structurally cannot.

answer.text: Language models reason about overall textual meaning and are not restricted by the graph acyclicity constraint that forces CollateX to split transpositions into deletions and insertions.

feedback.text: Correct. A model can recognize that a moved clause is the same text in a new position, testing whether semantic comprehension overcomes graph limitations.

answer.text: Language models automatically convert transpositions into Python bytecode scripts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Language models generate natural language and structured text, not bytecode.

answer.text: Variant graphs cannot process files that contain more than two sentences.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Variant graphs scale to entire books; the limitation is cyclic topology.

answer.text: Language models refuse to process omissions unless they are paired with transpositions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Models process any text supplied in the prompt.

questiontext.text: Why do deterministic algorithms like CollateX remain the scholarly gold standard for baseline collation despite the emerging capabilities of language models?

generalfeedback.text: A baseline needs to be reproducible before it needs to be clever — which is why deterministic alignment remains the standard.

answer.text: A baseline critical apparatus must be strictly reproducible, transparent, and re-derivable from stated rules before it needs to be clever.

feedback.text: Correct. Scholarly claims must be verifiable; a deterministic pipeline guarantees that identical input produces identical output every time.

answer.text: Deterministic algorithms require multimillion-dollar cloud supercomputer clusters to execute.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CollateX runs locally on standard laptops in fractions of a second.

answer.text: Language models are legally banned from academic publication by university presses.

feedback.text: Incorrect. AI tools are used across digital humanities, but require careful provenance and review.

answer.text: CollateX was invented in the 4th century CE and is protected by canon law.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CollateX is a modern open-source tool developed under the Interedition project.

questiontext.text: How does the risk profile of automated collation errors compare to manual collation errors?

generalfeedback.text: Automated collation fails systematically rather than randomly — uniform errors are invisible without a differently-produced baseline to compare against.

answer.text: Manual collation fails randomly due to sporadic fatigue, whereas automated collation fails systematically, creating uniform errors across every instance of an unencoded rule.

feedback.text: Correct. Systematic errors affect every matching pattern invisibly; comparing against an independent manual baseline is the only reliable way to detect them.

answer.text: Manual collation errors corrupt hard drive sectors, while automated errors damage RAM.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The risk profiles concern human attention lapses versus systematic software misconfiguration.

answer.text: Automated collation errors are always immediately obvious and color-coded in red.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Systematic errors produce uniformly plausible output that easily escapes notice.

answer.text: Manual collation produces zero errors if the editor drinks caffeinated tea.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Human cognitive fatigue is inevitable during sustained manual comparison.

questiontext.text: Why can two editors obtain completely different, yet equally valid, CollateX collations from the exact same manuscript witnesses?

generalfeedback.text: Different configurations produce different, equally correct collations of the same witnesses — only the method document says which question yours answers.

answer.text: Because each editor configures normalization rules and token definitions to answer a distinct research question (e.g. substantive variation vs. orthographic habit).

feedback.text: Correct. The algorithm simply executes the configuration it is given; the epistemological burden of defining what counts as a variant remains with the scholar.

answer.text: Because CollateX uses random number generators to determine alignment paths.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CollateX is fully deterministic; differences stem entirely from user configuration.

answer.text: Because Greek manuscripts change their Unicode encodings depending on the operating system.

feedback.text: Incorrect. UTF-8 Polytonic Greek encodings are standardized and stable.

answer.text: Because one editor is using an illegal pirated version of the CollateX library.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CollateX is open-source; differing outputs reflect differing philological policies.

questiontext.text: What three critical elements must be added to CollateX's raw export to transform it into Week 8's critical apparatus?

generalfeedback.text: Week 8 adds the lemma, the classification, and the formal sigla to today's export — the export is the raw material, not the apparatus.

answer.text: The adopted lemma (), the significance classification for filtering, and formal witness sigla declarations ().

feedback.text: Correct. Raw collation output merely records aligned readings; transforming it into an apparatus requires editorial lemma selection, taxonomy filtering, and formal header declarations.

answer.text: A copyright license, a CSS stylesheet, and a JavaScript event listener.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The missing elements are TEI apparatus structures and editorial judgements.

answer.text: English translations for every word, Latin morphological parses, and page numbers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. An apparatus criticus records textual variants and sigla, not interlinear translations.

answer.text: High-resolution JPEG images embedded directly inside every XML tag.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Facsimiles are linked via IIIF surfaces or coordinates, not embedded in apparatus tags.

name.text: 30 Question: Synthesis: Alignment Solved, Definition Not

questiontext.text: Why is sequence alignment considered a 'solved problem' while variant definition remains an active philological challenge?

generalfeedback.text: Alignment is solved; defining what counts as a variant is not, and that definition is the configuration you wrote today.

answer.text: Mathematical dynamic programming and graph models align strings flawlessly, but determining which differences constitute meaningful variants requires human domain expertise.

feedback.text: Correct. Needleman–Wunsch, Gotoh gap penalties, and variant graphs solve alignment; defining tokens and significance is the ongoing work of textual scholarship.

answer.text: Because all medieval manuscripts have already been collated and published in definitive print editions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Thousands of manuscript traditions remain uncollated; computational tools assist new work.

answer.text: Because computers can automatically discern divine inspiration from scribal corruption.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Computers have no semantic or theological discernment.

answer.text: Because variant definition was permanently standardized by the Council of Nicaea in 325 CE.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editorial principles and variant taxonomies are modern philological methods.
